candidate_relations.reason: Brainstem audiometry confirms profound right-sided hearing loss caused by temporal-bone involvement, not the underlying histiocytic disease.
Osteolysis is bilateral and also affects the left parietal bone, extending beyond a localized petrous apicitis.
Middle-ear effusion was an early clinical manifestation, but multifocal destructive skull lesions cannot be reduced to otitis media.
Paget disease is exceptional at age four and produces remodeling and expansion rather than these punched-out temporal and parietal lesions.
Purulent secretion and mastoid destruction can mimic mastoiditis, but bilateral labyrinthine osteolysis plus a separate parietal lesion indicates a systemic bone process.
There are no fractures, blue sclerae, or generalized osteopenia, and the lesions are focal osteolytic defects.
Otitis media with effusion was documented months earlier but does not explain progressive focal skull osteolysis and polypoid canal tissue.
Mild sinus mucosal thickening is incidental to the destructive mastoid, semicircular-canal, and parietal-bone lesions.
Eustachian dysfunction could contribute to effusion but cannot account for the CT-demonstrated multifocal osteolysis or severe asymmetric hearing loss.
Gorham-Stout disease can cause progressive osteolysis, but this child's multifocal temporal and skull lesions with ear-canal granulation fit the reference histiocytosis pattern.
The three-month ear history and canal secretion represent local disease, while the distant left parietal lesion remains unexplained by chronic otitis alone.
The child is alert with an age-appropriate neurologic examination and has skull-bone destruction rather than unilateral cerebral atrophy or seizures.
Fibrous dysplasia produces ground-glass expansion, not bilateral destructive mastoid and semicircular-canal lesions with a separate punched-out skull focus.
Otosclerosis causes abnormal bone deposition and conductive loss rather than frank osteolysis in a four-year-old.
Unsteadiness and falls suggest vestibular involvement, but absent nystagmus and extensive bony lysis make isolated labyrinthitis insufficient.
Adenoid hypertrophy appears on CT but does not produce parietal and temporal-bone osteolysis.
The duplicated Paget label conflicts with the patient's preschool age and the multifocal lytic rather than remodeling appearance.
Eosinophilic granuloma is the localized osseous form of Langerhans cell disease and fits a lytic skull lesion, but this case has multifocal bilateral temporal and parietal involvement.
No enhancing invasive epithelial mass is reported; the right canal polyp accompanies multifocal bone lysis in a child.
There are no seizures, focal cortical deficits, or hemispheric MRI abnormalities to support Rasmussen syndrome.

case_quality_flags: No tissue biopsy, CD1a/langerin staining, or Birbeck granule evidence is included to confirm Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
